transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello, Ms. Nakamura. Thank you for meeting with me again.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Hi. I've been reading about ABO incompatibility and transfusion reactions on my phone since we last spoke.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand you have a lot of questions. Before we dive into those, I want to start by saying again how sorry I am. It was my responsibility to ensure your blood type was verified before the transfusion, and I failed to do that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You said it was compatible, but not ideal. What does that actually mean? Like, why does it matter if it works?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a fair question. Essentially, there are different types of blood, and while we gave you blood that wouldn't cause a dangerous, immediate reaction, it wasn't your exact match. It’s like using a part for a car that fits and works, but isn't the specific brand recommended for your exact model.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But if it's not the exact match, isn't there a risk that my body will attack it now? I'm reading here that antibodies can cause hemolysis.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is completely understandable that you feel scared seeing terms like that online. When you're in a hospital for the first time and you see words like hemolysis, it feels like something is going wrong inside you right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It does. I just feel like I can't trust the process if something this basic was skipped.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize that the trust is broken. I took a shortcut in the verification process, and that is inexcusable. I am deeply sorry for the anxiety this is causing you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So, what happens now? Do I have to have another transfusion to fix this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, you don't need another transfusion. The blood we gave you is already being processed by your body. Because it was compatible, we don't expect any long-term complications, but we are going to monitor you closely to be sure.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Monitor how?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are going to draw your blood every twelve hours for the next two days to check your hemoglobin levels and look for any signs of those antibodies you mentioned.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And who is doing that? Are you doing it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will be overseeing the labs, but I have also briefed the attending physician and the head nurse. They are both aware of the error and are double-checking every single order for your care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is this how it usually happens? That people just skip the check?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It shouldn't. It is a strict protocol for a reason. To make sure this doesn't happen to anyone else, I've already filed an incident report, and our department is holding a mandatory review meeting tomorrow to change how the checklist is signed off.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just don't know if I can stop thinking about it. Every time I feel a chill or a headache, I'm wondering if it's the blood.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see how exhausting it is to be on high alert like that. It's a lot of pressure to put on yourself when you're already trying to recover from surgery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Exactly. I'm a grad student. I'm used to being the one with the answers, not the one wondering if the doctor forgot a step.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's a very jarring shift to feel like you have to be the one auditing your own care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So the blood tests. When will I get those results?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will come back to your room personally at 6:00 PM tonight to give you the results of the first set of labs.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Every twelve hours?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. Tonight at six, and then tomorrow morning at six.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. I'll keep my list of questions on my phone.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Please do. I want to make sure every concern you have is addressed. I'll see you at six.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts, allows the patient to express frustration and fear, and maintains a regulated pace throughout the encounter.

E.justification: The error (failure to verify blood type) is named explicitly and lay language is used, but there are no explicit checks for patient comprehension (e.g., 'Does that make sense?').

A.justification: The resident uses direct apology language, takes personal responsibility ('I failed to do that', 'I took a shortcut'), and maintains accountability under pushback.

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions ('scared', 'anxiety', 'exhausting') and validates the patient's specific experience as a grad student.

T.justification: The resident provides specific next steps (blood draws), clear timelines (6:00 PM tonight/tomorrow), a patient role (keeping the list of questions), and addresses prevention (incident report/review meeting).
